Jeoparded
JEP-ar-ded
v. (past tense; hazarded, exposed to deadly risk)
From Old French jeu parti, a divided game, an even chance, hence a hazard. Jeopard is the older verb, now displaced by jeopardize. The Hebrew charaph here means to expose or cast down, to despise one's own life for a cause.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In the song of Deborah the tribes are reviewed one by one, and the honour roll is short: “Zebulun and Naphtali were a people that jeoparded their lives unto the death in the high places of the field” (Judges 5:18). To jeopard a life is to put it at even hazard, to throw it where it may well be lost. Zebulun and Naphtali came down to Kishon when Barak called, and the song does not praise their success but their willingness to die. Set against them stands Meroz: “Curse ye Meroz, said the angel of the LORD, curse ye bitterly the inhabitants thereof; because they came not to the help of the LORD, to the help of the LORD against the mighty” (Judges 5:23). The dividing line in the song is not between brave men and cowards in the abstract but between those who answered the LORD's call at cost and those who stayed by their flocks and ships. The whole principle is gathered up and perfected in Christ, who did not merely jeopard His life but laid it down: “Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): JEOPARD, to hazard; to put in danger; to expose to loss or injury.

expand to see more

JEOPARD, v.t. To hazard; to put in danger; to expose to loss or injury.

JEOPARDY, n. Exposure to death, loss or injury; hazard; danger; peril.

From Old French jeu parti, a divided or even game, hence a hazard.

Judges 5:18 praises Zebulun and Naphtali, who jeoparded their lives unto the death.

The form jeoparded has been displaced by jeopardized.

Key Scripture

Jdg 5:18 — "Zebulun and Naphtali were a people that jeoparded their lives unto the death in the high places of the field."

Jdg 5:23 — "Curse ye Meroz, said the angel of the LORD, curse ye bitterly the inhabitants thereof; because they came not to the help of the LORD, to the help of the LORD against the mighty."

Joh 15:13 — "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends."

Modern Corruption

Costly obedience is downgraded to a lifestyle option, so that the believer who risks nothing is told he is simply honouring his own boundaries.

expand to see more

A church shaped by the vocabulary of self-care has little room for a people that jeoparded their lives unto the death. Risk is reframed as poor stewardship of the self, and the refusal to come down to the battle is dignified as the setting of a healthy limit. Meroz is no longer cursed; Meroz is commended for knowing its own capacity.

Scripture keeps the harder categories. The angel of the LORD curses the tribe that stayed home, and the song honours the tribes that went. The call is not to recklessness, and the believer owes real duties to family and calling; but Deborah's song and the cross together forbid the doctrine that a Christian owes God nothing he is unwilling to lose. He who laid down His life for His friends has every right to ask the risk of His people.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From jeu parti, an even game or hazard; Judges 5:18 honours the tribes that hazarded their lives unto the death.

expand to see more

Old French jeu parti, a divided game, an even chance, hence a hazard.

Hebrew charaph here means to expose or despise one's own life for a cause.

Judges 5:18 is the only occurrence of jeoparded in the Authorized Version.

Meroz is cursed in the same song for refusing the same call (Judges 5:23).

Christ did not jeopard but laid down His life (John 15:13).

Usage

"marks costly obedience to the LORD's call"

"stands in the song over against the curse upon Meroz"
